Social across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Between ages 5 and 7, social cognition undergoes a marked qualitative shift from understanding isolated mental states to basic reasoning about nested social representations and navigating increasingly complex peer ecologies. Theory of mind advances beyond first-order false belief (what another person thinks) toward second-order reasoning (what one person thinks another person thinks), with most children passing classic second-order false-belief tasks (e.g understanding that "John thinks Mary thinks the ice cream van is in the park") between 6 and 7 years 1, 2, a capacity that requires holding and manipulating nested propositional attitudes and predicts more sophisticated social problem-solving and peer acceptance (and continues to develop for many more years). Children also develop basic interpretive theory of mind: they come to understand that two people witnessing the same event can form different beliefs about it depending on their prior knowledge, attention, or interpretive frameworks 3, 4, 5, moving beyond the simpler realization that people can hold false beliefs to grasping that beliefs are actively constructed rather than passively received (which relates to the emergence of metalinguistic awareness at this stage). This supports more nuanced social navigation, as six- and seven-year-olds increasingly recognize that disagreements can stem from differing interpretations rather than one party simply being wrong, and they begin to adjust their communication strategies accordingly (e.g explaining more when they detect that a listener lacks relevant background or holds a different construal). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Emotion understanding deepens in parallel, with children gaining firmer mastery of display rules (the social norms governing when and how to express or mask feelings) and applying them more flexibly across contexts: whereas five-year-olds show emerging awareness that people can hide feelings, six- and seven-year-olds can reliably predict when someone would display a false emotion (e.g smiling when receiving a disappointing gift) and can articulate the social motivations behind such regulation 6, 7, 8, indicating integration of emotion knowledge with normative and strategic reasoning. They also develop more sophisticated causal models of emotion, moving from simple situational attributions ("she’s sad because her toy broke") to incorporating beliefs, desires, and past history ("he’s angry because he thought his friend would save him a seat, and they’ve had arguments before") 9, and they begin to understand self-conscious emotions like pride, shame, embarrassment, and guilt as distinct from basic emotions, recognizing that these require an evaluative self-representation and tracking others’ judgments. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Peer relationships undergo structural and functional reorganization during this window. Friendships shift from activity-based and relatively transient ("we’re friends because we play together") toward more stable, psychologically grounded bonds; six- and seven-year-olds increasingly cite personality traits, shared interests, and reciprocal liking as friendship criteria 10, 11, and friendship stability (maintaining the same best friend over months) rises relative to preschool. Cooperative play becomes more rule-governed and competitive-cooperative, with games involving explicit turn-taking, scorekeeping, and negotiated rule modifications 12, 13, 14, and children show heightened sensitivity to fairness violations and procedural justice within peer interactions 15, 16, both protesting unfair treatment (and unfair group norms 17, 18) more vigorously and invoking equity norms to resolve disputes (although still unreliably).

Moral and prosocial reasoning also advance. While five-year-olds show strong fairness preferences in simple allocation tasks, some six- and seven-year-olds integrate multiple moral dimensions: they consider not only equality but also merit (rewarding harder work), and need (giving more to those who lack), and they increasingly balance self-interest against group welfare when these conflict 19, 20, 15, 21, 22 (though this behavior is far from robust/solidified; it is strictly emerging at this stage, which most children either being fully self-interested or using "equal shares" heuristics). Prosocial behavior becomes more strategic and reputation-sensitive: helping and sharing increase in public relative to private contexts 23, 24, and children selectively assist peers who have helped others (indirect reciprocity) or who might reciprocate in the future 25, 26, indicating that prosocial acts are now partly governed by reputational and reciprocal incentives rather than purely empathic motivation.

Group dynamics become more salient and hierarchically structured. By early elementary school, peer networks exhibit clear social hierarchies, with some children consistently preferred as playmates and leaders, and children are acutely aware of their own and others’ social standing, actively working to maintain or improve their position through strategic affiliation, selective disclosure, and sometimes exclusion or relational aggression 27, 28, 29. Gender segregation typically intensifies across this period, with children increasingly preferring same-gender playmates and engaging in gender-typed activities, driven by a combination of identity development, peer enforcement of gender norms, and differential socialization pressures. Friendship networks also begin to cluster into stable cliques or groups with shared norms and coordinated activities, and being accepted into a desirable peer group becomes a central social goal 30.

Collectively, these shifts reflect a social-cognitive system that is no longer merely tracking individual minds but is beginning to actively model the social field (its reputational dynamics, normative structures, relational networks, and emergent hierarchies), preparing children to navigate the increasingly complex and competitive social ecologies of middle childhood.
